The other door

I came to the art market through the other door.

Most dealers arrive from a gallery or an auction house. I arrived from the law and the trading floor.

I trained in legal cost assessment in Edinburgh and the City of London, where the job was to test every figure and every claim. I went on to trade my own account in equities and derivatives, where I learned how fast a price can run ahead of its value. Through all of it, for more than thirty years, I have bought contemporary art for my own walls.

That combination shapes how I look at a painting. I ask what it is worth, who says so, and what happens if they are wrong.

How I assess an artist

Five questions I ask before I recommend any work.

A record price set on one evening is not a market. Across 185 research papers, the same lesson keeps returning: prices hold best where museums and serious galleries arrived before the speculators. So these are the questions I ask first.

  1. Who has committed to the artist?

    Museum exhibitions and permanent collections count for more than headlines.

  2. Who represents them, and how?

    A good gallery places work carefully and protects its artists from quick resales.

  3. What does the auction record really say?

    I look past the record to the depth of sales, repeat sales, buyer’s premium and the currency the price was set in.

  4. What is the condition and the paper trail?

    Provenance, exhibition history, invoices and condition reports decide what a work is worth when you come to sell.

  5. Is it a good work by this artist?

    Not every work by a celebrated name is a strong one. Date, scale and quality matter as much as the signature.

The research library

The research is published, so you can check it.

Every artist I discuss has been researched in depth, and the work is on this site for anyone to read. About

Al Miller

Collector first. Dealer second. Analyst always.

I am an independent contemporary art dealer and financial communication specialist, born in Scotland. I bought my first serious work of art more than thirty years ago, because I loved it. Everything since has taught me how to make sure love and judgment point in the same direction.

Book a conversation

1980s
Edinburgh and the City

A training in testing every figure

I trained in legal cost assessment in Edinburgh in the 1980s, then worked in the City of London through the late 1980s and 1990s on cases for larger firms.

Cost law is an unglamorous discipline with one great lesson: a number is only as good as the evidence behind it.

I still work that way. When a gallery quotes a price or an auction house publishes a record, my first question is what supports it.

The trading screens

Learning how markets behave

After the law I traded my own account in equities and derivatives. Trading teaches you things no textbook does: that prices overshoot in both directions, that liquidity disappears exactly when you need it, and that the difference between price and value is where most money is lost.

The contemporary art market behaves in the same way, only more slowly and with less information. That is why I read it with a trader’s caution.

Dimensions

Explaining markets in plain English

In the early 2000s I founded and published Dimensions, an investment magazine. Writing for readers who wanted the truth about markets, without jargon, gave me the habit I bring to everything I write now, from a research paper on a young painter to a Consumer Duty report for an advice firm.

Thirty years of collecting

Thirty years on the buyer’s side

I have collected contemporary art for more than three decades, with my own money and for my own walls. That matters, because it means I have always sat where my clients sit: weighing a work I want against a price I have to justify.

It also means I know what the trade does not volunteer. How a work was acquired, how many similar ones are waiting to come to market, what a condition report leaves unsaid, what it will really cost to sell. Those are the questions I answer for clients before they buy.

The research

Why I publish my research

I have written 185 research papers and 150 Market Insight articles, and they are all on this site. Most cover individual artists, from established names to painters in their twenties. Others deal with the practical side of collecting: editions, condition, insurance, moving art across borders and passing it on.

I publish them for a simple reason. If you are going to trust my judgment, you should be able to see how I reach it.

Read the research

How I work

Five principles

Independent

I am not tied to any gallery, auction house or fund. If anyone else pays me in connection with a work, I tell you.

Selective

I work with a small number of collectors and artists at a time, so each gets proper attention.

Evidence-led

Every recommendation comes with written reasoning that you can check.

Plain-spoken

I will tell you when a work is overpriced, when to wait and when to walk away.

Honest about risk

Works of art are not regulated investments. Prices fall as well as rise, and selling can take time. I will never tell you otherwise.

Financial communication

Why a collector writes for advice firms

Alongside the art, I write for FCA-authorised advice firms: client guides, market commentary and the Consumer Duty documents that firms must be able to stand behind, from Fair Value Assessments to Annual Board Reports.

It is the same skill applied to a different subject. Regulated communication must be clear to clients and precise enough for compliance. My training in cost law and my years in the markets give me both.
